topic: What belongs in an ADR Context section
stem: What must the Context section of an architecture decision record capture?

options.text: The forces in effect at the time — constraints, deadlines, team capacity — including those too obvious to write down.
A description of the system architecture as it stood immediately before the decision, component by component.
The business justification for the programme the decision sits within, as set out in the funding case.
The stakeholders consulted before the choice, and the position each of them took on the options.

explanation.correct: Decisions are rational relative to their circumstances, and the circumstances are what evaporate. A reader two years later sees a choice that looks wrong without knowing there were three engineers, a regulatory deadline and a data-access approval still outstanding. The obvious-at-the-time forces are the ones most often omitted and most often needed, because they are precisely the ones that will have changed. Recording them is what lets a future reader distinguish a decision that has expired from one that was never sound.

distractors.B: The prior architecture belongs in the design documentation, and it describes state rather than pressure. Knowing what the system looked like does not tell a reader why one option was viable and another was not.
distractors.C: Programme justification sits in the business case and is usually stable across many decisions. Repeating it in every record adds length without helping anyone judge whether this particular choice still holds.
distractors.D: Who was consulted is useful provenance and worth capturing somewhere, but positions taken are not forces. A record listing opinions without the constraints that shaped them explains politics rather than engineering.

explanation.concept: An ADR's Context records the forces acting at the moment of decision, especially the ones that seemed self-evident then. Those constraints are what a future reader must test to judge whether the decision has expired, and they are unrecoverable if not written down.
explanation.tip: Ask what a reader would need in order to conclude 'that was reasonable then, and it is not now'. Everything answering that question is Context; everything else belongs in another section or another document.

topic: Hard versus soft benefit in an AI business case
stem: In an AI business case, what distinguishes a hard benefit from a soft benefit?

options.text: A hard benefit can be measured objectively; a soft benefit is inherently unmeasurable and can only be asserted in the case.
A hard benefit removes a cost from a budget line; a soft benefit improves something real that no budget line records.
A hard benefit is realised inside the first year of operation; a soft benefit accrues over a longer horizon.
A hard benefit is guaranteed by a contract or a signed commitment; a soft benefit is an estimate.

explanation.correct: The test is whether a finance system will show the change. A cost avoided, a contractor role not filled, a licence retired — these land somewhere a budget owner can point to. Reduced frustration, faster onboarding or better decision quality can be perfectly real and even carefully measured, but nothing in the ledger moves. Keeping the two separate protects the credibility of the case: a benefit claimed as cash and never seen poisons the next three business cases the team brings.

distractors.A: Soft benefits are frequently measured, sometimes with more rigour than hard ones — cycle time, error rates and satisfaction all have instruments. Measurability is not the dividing line; visibility in the accounts is.
distractors.C: Timing is orthogonal. A hard saving can arrive in year three when a contract renews, and a soft benefit can appear the week after launch. Classifying by horizon confuses when a benefit lands with what kind of benefit it is.
distractors.D: Contractual guarantee is rare for either category and describes certainty rather than type. Most hard benefits are forecasts too; the difference is that when they materialise, they materialise in a budget.

explanation.concept: Hard benefits show up in a budget line; soft benefits are real improvements that no budget line records. Both belong in a case, stated separately, and a soft benefit converts to hard only via a named mechanism with an owner.
explanation.tip: The distinguishing question is not 'can we measure it' but 'will finance see it'. Options built on measurability or timing are describing something else.

topic: Why the internal objective is tighter than the agreement
stem: Why is an internal SLO normally set tighter than the SLA it backs?

options.text: Because internal teams need a stretch target above the contractual figure to maintain performance discipline.
Because SLAs are measured over longer windows than SLOs, so the tighter internal figure compensates for that averaging.
Because external auditors require two distinct thresholds for every externally committed service.
Because the gap is a warning margin: crossing the internal target pulls attention while the commitment is intact.

explanation.correct: The two thresholds do different jobs. The contractual one defines when the organisation owes something; the internal one has to fire early enough that the team can act before that happens. Setting them equal means the first signal that anything is wrong is a breach, which leaves no room to investigate, remediate or communicate. The size of the gap is itself a design decision — it should be wide enough to cover the time from detection to fix for the failure modes the team actually experiences.

distractors.A: Stretch targets are a management device, and a target set purely for motivation gets discounted by everyone who reads it. The internal objective needs a specific operational function, which is to leave time before a contractual event.
distractors.B: Window lengths vary in both directions and are set independently of the target. Even with identical windows the internal objective would still need to be tighter, so averaging cannot be the reason.
distractors.C: No such general audit requirement exists. Where regulators do take an interest, it is in whether the service met its commitments and whether breaches were handled, not in how many thresholds the team maintains.

explanation.concept: Set the internal objective tighter than the external commitment by a margin sized to the time it takes to detect and remediate. The gap converts a contractual event into an engineering signal, which is the only way a breach becomes preventable rather than merely reportable.
explanation.tip: Whenever an item pairs an internal and an external threshold, the reason for the gap is response time. Options invoking motivation, audit mandates or measurement windows are all describing something else.

topic: What being well calibrated means over many statements
stem: A team describes its architect as well calibrated. Assessed over a long series of statements, what does that mean?

options.text: The architect's estimates usually land close to the outcome that eventually occurs.
Among the statements made with 80% confidence, close to 80% turned out to be true.
The architect never states a confidence level without documented evidence to support it.
The architect's estimates are deliberately conservative, so actual outcomes usually beat them.

explanation.correct: Calibration is a property of the confidence levels, not of the predictions. It is assessed by bucketing statements by the confidence attached to them and checking whether the hit rate in each bucket matches the label. This is why calibration can only be judged across many statements, and why it is a distinct virtue from being right: someone who is right 95% of the time but says 'certain' every time is accurate and badly calibrated, because their 'certain' carries no information about which cases to check.

distractors.A: Being close to the outcome is accuracy. A forecaster can be highly accurate and still calibrated badly if the confidence attached to each statement bears no relation to how often that confidence level is borne out.
distractors.C: Evidential discipline is good practice and a plausible cause of calibration, but it is not what the term measures. A well-evidenced estimator who systematically overstates confidence is still miscalibrated.
distractors.D: Systematic conservatism is a bias, and biases are exactly what calibration detects. Someone whose 60% statements come true 90% of the time is under-confident, and their estimates cannot be used at face value either.

explanation.concept: Calibration means stated confidence matches observed frequency across many statements, and it can only be assessed in aggregate. It is independent of accuracy: consistent over-confidence and consistent under-confidence are both miscalibration, and both make the estimates unusable for allocating scrutiny.
explanation.tip: Distinguish accuracy from calibration on sight. Accuracy is about individual predictions; calibration is about whether the confidence labels mean anything when grouped.

topic: Why fine-tuning cannot keep answers factually current
stem: Why does fine-tuning fail to keep a system's answers factually current?

options.text: Because knowledge in weights is fixed at training time and changes only on retraining, while the facts keep moving.
Because fine-tuned models lose the ability to follow instructions about preferring recent information.
Because fine-tuning datasets cannot contain dated material such as effective-from timestamps.
Because a fine-tuned model cannot be combined with a retrieval layer that supplies it with current facts at request time.

explanation.correct: Weights are a snapshot. Every fact encoded into them is frozen at the moment of training, and correcting a single one means assembling data and running training again — a cycle measured in weeks, against facts that may change daily. Retrieval inverts that economics: correcting a fact is an index update, and the correction takes effect on the next request. This is why currency is a retrieval concern regardless of how much fine-tuning is done, and why a fine-tune aimed at freshness buys a problem that recurs forever.

distractors.B: Instruction-following is not what breaks. A tuned model can be told to prefer recent information and will comply — it simply has no recent information to prefer unless something supplies it at request time.
distractors.C: Training data routinely contains dated material, and dating it does not help. The issue is not that the model cannot represent time; it is that nothing updates the representation between training runs.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning and retrieval combine perfectly well, and the combination is often the right design — tuned behaviour with retrieved facts. The claim that they are incompatible is simply false.

explanation.concept: Weights hold behaviour; context holds facts. Anything that changes on a shorter cycle than your retraining cadence must arrive through retrieval or tool calls, because the cost of correcting a fact in weights is a training run and the cost of correcting it in an index is an update.
explanation.tip: Sort any 'fine-tune or retrieve' question by change frequency. If the thing in question changes faster than you can retrain, retrieval is the answer regardless of budget.

topic: The run-cost line that does not amortise with volume
stem: In a Claude-based system with a mandatory human review step, which cost fails to amortise as processed volume grows?

options.text: The build cost of the integration with the surrounding operational systems.
The cost of maintaining and re-labelling the evaluation set as the task changes.
The cost of developing, reviewing and versioning the prompt library.
Human review, incurred per item and therefore rising in step with volume.

explanation.correct: Per-item costs do not get cheaper with scale — they get bigger. This is what makes mandatory review the line that decides whether a business case survives contact with production volume, because the benefit is usually modelled as scaling while the review cost is quietly assumed to be fixed. It also determines the shape of the right optimisation: the lever is reducing the proportion of items needing review, or the minutes each takes, not spreading a fixed cost over more units.

distractors.A: Integration is built once and then serves whatever volume arrives, so its contribution per processed item falls continuously as throughput rises. That is the definition of amortising, and it is why one-off build cost rarely constrains how large a system can profitably grow.
distractors.B: Eval maintenance tracks how often the task, the policy or the model changes, not how many items pass through. Doubling volume with a stable task leaves the maintenance effort roughly where it was.
distractors.C: Prompt development and versioning are driven by change cadence and by the number of distinct tasks, not by request count. The same prompt library serves ten thousand or ten million requests at the same cost.

explanation.concept: Separate per-item costs from per-change and one-off costs when modelling an AI system at scale. Human review and inference scale with volume; build, prompt engineering and eval maintenance amortise. Only the per-item lines constrain how large the system can profitably become.
explanation.tip: Classify every cost line by what it scales with: volume, rate of change, or nothing. The volume-scaled lines are the ones that decide whether the case holds at full rollout.

topic: What makes a head-to-head model comparison decision-grade
stem: What makes a head-to-head comparison of two models decision-grade for a production system?

options.text: Both are evaluated on the same public benchmark under identical settings, with the same scoring script applied to each.
Both run on the same task-specific eval set with comparable tuning effort, and latency, output format and safety measured on both.
Both are given the incumbent's tuned production prompt unchanged, so neither candidate receives special treatment.
The challenger is evaluated on the cases where the incumbent currently fails, since that is where any improvement would have to show up.

explanation.correct: A comparison drives a decision only if it measures the thing the decision turns on and gives both candidates a fair run at it. That means the organisation's own eval set rather than a general benchmark, comparable tuning effort so the result reflects the models rather than the effort invested, and the non-quality axes included — a challenger that scores higher but misses the latency budget or breaks the output contract is not actually a candidate. Leave any of those out and the comparison produces a number without producing a decision.

distractors.A: A shared public benchmark makes the comparison fair and irrelevant. It measures a task distribution that is not yours, so the ranking it produces need not survive contact with your own data, rubric and edge cases.
distractors.C: Using the incumbent's prompt unchanged sounds even-handed and is systematically biased: that prompt embeds months of tuning against one model's quirks. Equal treatment means comparable effort on each side, not identical text.
distractors.D: Testing only on the incumbent's failures measures the marginal case and hides regressions. A challenger can fix half those failures while breaking cases the incumbent handled, and this design would never see it.

explanation.concept: Decision-grade comparison requires your own eval set, comparable tuning effort per candidate, and the non-quality requirements measured alongside quality. Reusing the incumbent's tuned prompt or testing only on its failures both bias the result in ways that survive into production.
explanation.tip: Watch for options that equate fairness with identical inputs. Giving both models the same prompt is not equal treatment when that prompt was fitted to one of them.

topic: Writing a decision record at the time of the decision
stem: Why should an architecture decision record be written when the decision is taken rather than reconstructed afterwards?

options.text: Because the information and constraints present when choosing are the record's substance and cannot be recovered later.
Because the organisation's governance framework requires design documentation to exist before implementation begins.
Because reconstructing the record later takes considerably more effort than writing it at the time.
Because the decision cannot be implemented until the record has been reviewed and approved.

explanation.correct: A record written after the fact is written by someone who knows how it turned out, and hindsight silently rewrites what was uncertain into what was obvious. Options that were genuinely live get dropped because they now look foolish; constraints that shaped the choice get forgotten because they have since lifted. What remains is a justification rather than a decision record, and it is useless for the one job the artefact has — letting a future reader judge whether the reasoning still applies.

distractors.B: Some organisations do impose documentation gates, but that is a local policy rather than the reason. A record produced only to clear a gate is exactly the kind that gets written retrospectively and carries no reasoning.
distractors.C: Effort is a secondary consideration and sometimes runs the other way, since a retrospective record can be shorter. The problem with writing late is that the content is wrong, not that it is expensive.
distractors.D: Decision records are not approval instruments. Blocking implementation on them confuses an ADR with a change-control gate and encourages teams to write them as compliance paperwork after the work is already done.

explanation.concept: Write the record at the point of decision, because its value lies in preserving the uncertainty that existed then. Hindsight compresses live options into obvious ones and drops the constraints that made the choice hard, which is precisely the information a later reader needs.
explanation.tip: The reason to write early is always epistemic, not procedural. Options citing governance gates, effort or approval workflow are describing organisational habits rather than what the artefact is for.

topic: Committing to escalation time instead of accuracy
stem: Why is 'time to a human decision when the system defers' often a better contractual commitment than an output accuracy figure?

options.text: Because it is cheaper for the supplier to guarantee than any output accuracy figure would be.
Because accuracy is a property of the model and therefore the model provider's responsibility rather than the integrator's.
Because it is measurable from timestamps and bounds the customer's worst case however the model performs on an item.
Because customers in practice care more about speed of resolution than about the correctness of the answer.

explanation.correct: It commits to the property the customer actually needs — that no case gets stuck — and it does so in a form that telemetry can settle without adjudication. It is also robust in the way an accuracy clause is not: if the model performs worse than expected, deferral volume rises and the commitment still holds, because it constrains the escalation path rather than the model. That makes it a term the supplier can honour under bad conditions, which is the only kind of term worth signing.

distractors.A: Cost of compliance is not the argument, and a tight escalation target can be expensive since it requires staffed human capacity. The case rests on measurability and on what the commitment protects.
distractors.B: The integrator owns the behaviour of the system it sells, whatever component produces the output. Disclaiming accuracy as the provider's problem would not survive a customer conversation and is not why the escalation term is preferable.
distractors.D: Customers care about both, and in most regulated settings correctness dominates. The point is not that speed matters more, but that a bounded escalation path protects the customer even when correctness varies.

explanation.concept: Where the primary attribute cannot be measured per instance, commit to a bound on the failure path instead. Escalation time is timestamped, verifiable without adjudication, and remains honourable when model performance degrades — which is when contractual terms are tested.
explanation.tip: In SLA items, prefer the commitment that stays achievable under bad conditions. A term that only holds while the model behaves well is a term that breaches exactly when it matters.

topic: Recording a decision taken under deadline with partial evidence
stem: A payments company had four days to choose between two integration approaches for its Claude-based dispute-narrative service before a card scheme deadline, and chose on partial evidence. Two weeks later the architect is writing the ADR. Which THREE things must the record state? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: That the choice was made against a four-day scheme deadline, and which evidence was consequently not gathered.
The evidence that would have been gathered with more time, and whether gathering it now would still change anything.
The outcome over the two weeks since go-live, presented as confirmation that the choice was sound.
The revisit trigger — what observation would cause the team to reopen the choice now the deadline has passed.
An acknowledgement of the process shortfall and a commitment to allow adequate time on future decisions of this kind.

explanation.correct: A decision taken under time pressure is not a bad decision, but it is a decision with a known gap, and the record's job is to make that gap explicit rather than to hide it. Naming the deadline and the evidence forgone tells a future reader how much weight the reasoning carries. Naming what would have been gathered, and whether it is still worth gathering, converts the gap into an actionable item rather than a permanent asterisk. And the revisit trigger is what stops an expedient choice quietly hardening into a permanent one.

distractors.C: Two weeks of uneventful operation is weak evidence and belongs nowhere near the record's reasoning. Using outcome to validate a decision also teaches exactly the wrong lesson, since a decision taken on inadequate evidence can turn out well by luck.
distractors.E: Process commitments belong in a retrospective, not in a decision record. An ADR captures a technical choice and its consequences; mixing in organisational undertakings makes it a document nobody knows how to maintain or supersede.

explanation.concept: When a decision is forced by a deadline, record the constraint, the evidence forgone, and the trigger for revisiting. Time pressure is a legitimate force to document; what is illegitimate is a record that presents an expedient choice as a fully evidenced one.
explanation.tip: Retrospective-ADR items reliably include an outcome-as-vindication distractor and a process-improvement distractor. Both are real things teams write, and neither belongs in the record.

topic: Qualifying a saving from a model tier downgrade
stem: A media monitoring company routed 70% of its Claude-based article-tagging traffic from the higher capability tier to a cheaper one and reports a 44% reduction in monthly inference spend to its executive team. Which TWO things must accompany that figure for it to be a decision-grade claim? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A commitment that no traffic will be routed back to the higher tier, so the saving is durable across quarters and can be booked in the budget.
The measured quality delta on the eval set for the traffic that moved, so the saving can be weighed against its quality cost.
The share of the company's overall cloud and data-platform spend that inference now represents after the reroute.
The definition of the routing rule that selects the 70%, since the saving holds only while the traffic mix resembles the calibration set.
An assurance from the provider that the cheaper tier will remain available for the life of the service contract.

explanation.correct: A cost reduction on a quality-bearing system is half a number. The quality delta on exactly the traffic that moved is the other half, and without it the executive team is approving a saving whose price is invisible. The routing rule matters because the 44% is a property of the current mix: if the share of articles the rule sends to the cheaper tier drifts, the saving drifts with it, and nobody will know why. Stating both turns a headline into something that can be monitored and revisited.

distractors.A: Promising never to route back removes the safety valve. If quality on some article class turns out unacceptable, escalating that class to the higher tier is the correct response, and a durability commitment would forbid it.
distractors.C: Proportional context is interesting for prioritising attention and says nothing about whether this particular saving is real or what it cost. A claim is not made decision-grade by being placed next to a larger number.
distractors.E: Availability assurances address a supply risk that applies equally before and after the change. They do not qualify the measured saving, and they would not tell the executive team anything about the trade-off just made.

explanation.concept: Any cost reduction achieved by lowering capability must be reported with the measured quality delta on the affected traffic and the routing condition under which the saving holds. A saving quoted without its quality price and its validity condition is not a finding.
explanation.tip: Cost-optimisation claims always have two hidden dimensions: what quality it cost, and under what traffic assumption it holds. The keys are the options that supply those; the rest supply comfort.

topic: Conditions for quoting an accuracy figure in a tender
stem: A clinical-documentation vendor's sales lead wants to quote '94% accuracy' for its Claude-based discharge-letter summariser in a hospital tender response. Which TWO conditions must hold before that figure goes into the document? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The figure travels with the population measured, the sample size, the date, and the model and prompt versions in effect.
The response states that the figure is indicative only, which removes any need to describe how it was produced.
The figure has been independently reproduced by a third-party clinical auditor and certified before the response is submitted.
The same figure has already been achieved on the tendering hospital's own document mix and case load, measured before submission.
The grading rubric is stated, since accuracy for a clinical letter summary is a rubric judgement, not an objective match.

explanation.correct: A quality number quoted to a customer becomes a representation, so it has to carry enough context to be checkable and to remain true. Population, sample size, date and versions are what let a reader know what the figure describes and when it goes stale — a number measured on one document type under a prompt since revised describes nothing current. The rubric matters because there is no objective ground truth for a summary: 94% is 94% against someone's definition of adequate, and without that definition the figure is not a measurement, it is a claim.

distractors.B: An indicative label does not cure an unexplained number, and it is not obvious it would protect the vendor if a hospital relied on it. Disclaiming a figure while still quoting it is the worst of both — no assurance for the buyer, no clarity for anyone.
distractors.C: Independent verification is a strong differentiator where a buyer demands it, and is not a precondition for stating a measurement honestly. Making it mandatory would mean no vendor could ever quote its own results.
distractors.D: The vendor does not have the hospital's documents, so this cannot be satisfied before submission. It is worth offering as a proof-of-concept commitment in the response, but it cannot gate whether an existing measurement may be quoted.

explanation.concept: A quality figure quoted externally must carry its population, sample size, date, system versions and grading rubric. Where the metric involves judgement, the rubric is part of the number — the same output can score very differently under two defensible definitions of correct.
explanation.tip: For any externally quoted metric, ask what would have to be true for it to still be accurate in six months. Provenance and rubric are the two things that make that answerable.

topic: Answering a regulator with a stale accuracy measurement
stem: In a supervisory meeting, a financial regulator asks the architect what the accuracy of the firm's Claude-based suitability-assessment summariser is. The most recent measurement, 0.91, comes from an eval run eleven months ago, against a model version that has since changed twice and a prompt that has been revised three times. The architect must answer in the room. What should the answer be?

options.text: Give 0.91 as the firm's accuracy figure, noting that it is the most recent measurement the eval programme has produced.
Give 0.91, note that it predates two model changes and three prompt revisions and so does not describe today's system, and commit to a remeasurement date.
Decline to give any figure in the room, on the basis that quoting a stale number to a regulator is worse than saying nothing.
Give 0.91 and add that the model changes and prompt revisions since were improvements, so current accuracy is at least that.

explanation.correct: The supervisor is testing whether the firm knows the state of its own controls, and the honest answer contains both what is known and the boundary of that knowledge. Naming the changes since the measurement is what converts a number into an assessment, and it pre-empts the far worse outcome of the regulator discovering the staleness later. Committing to a date and to a written follow-up turns an uncomfortable admission into evidence of control, which is precisely what a supervisor is looking for.

distractors.A: Offering the figure without the caveat lets the regulator record 0.91 as the current control effectiveness. When the divergence emerges, the issue is no longer the measurement gap but whether the firm's disclosures can be relied on.
distractors.C: Silence withholds information the firm holds and signals either evasion or disorganisation. The regulator can see the figure exists in the firm's records; refusing to characterise it invites a broader review.
distractors.D: Asserting that accuracy is at least 0.91 is an unmeasured claim about a control, made to a supervisor. Prompt revisions and version changes routinely move quality in both directions, and this is the answer most likely to become a finding.

explanation.concept: Report a stale measurement with its date, the changes since, and a commitment to remeasure. Never extrapolate an unmeasured improvement, and never withhold a figure that exists. Supervisors assess whether an organisation knows the limits of its own evidence.
explanation.tip: When a stem lists changes made since the last measurement, it is signalling that the caveat is the answer. Both extremes — quoting bare and refusing to quote — are traps.

topic: Correcting a launch claim against measured deferral rates
stem: A pet insurer's marketing team wants the launch page for its Claude-based claims assistant to read 'instant decisions on every claim'. In production, 22% of claims are deferred to a human assessor with a stated two-working-day turnaround, and a further 4% are stopped by a guardrail and re-routed. Launch is in six days. What is the best next step?

options.text: Approve the copy: 74% of claims do receive an instant decision, and launch copy is understood to describe the intended experience rather than a guarantee.
Ask marketing to drop every reference to decision speed and describe the assistant's capabilities in general terms instead of numbers.
Escalate the wording to the legal team for a view on whether it is misleading, and let them determine the final launch copy.
Give marketing accurate wording backed by the figures: instant decisions on around three quarters of claims, most of the rest within two working days.

explanation.correct: The claim is false as written for more than a quarter of claimants, and in insurance a public statement about decision speed sets an expectation a regulator and an ombudsman will both take seriously. The architect holds the one thing that resolves it quickly: the actual figures and a defensible way to express them. Supplying a specific alternative rather than an objection is what gets it fixed inside six days, and the honest version is still a good claim — three quarters instant, with the 22% deferred bounded at two working days, is a stronger promise than most competitors can make. Note that the wording must not extend that two-day bound to the 4% stopped by a guardrail, for whom the stem states no turnaround at all.

distractors.A: The 74% figure is exactly why the copy is wrong: over a quarter of claimants get no instant decision at all, most of them waiting up to two working days, after being told decisions are instant. Treating a factual claim about service levels as aspirational is how complaints and regulatory findings begin.
distractors.B: Stripping the speed claim discards a genuine strength and leaves marketing with vague copy they will resist. The problem is the word 'every', not the topic, and over-correcting makes the architect the obstacle rather than the source of the fix.
distractors.C: Legal review is worth having, but legal cannot assess or rewrite the claim without the deferral figures, which only the architect can supply. Handing over the question without the data consumes days of a six-day window and returns the same request.

explanation.concept: When a public claim conflicts with measured behaviour, supply the measurement and a specific accurate alternative rather than an objection or an escalation. The honest version of a service claim is usually still compelling, and it survives the first customer who experiences the exception.
explanation.tip: Universal quantifiers — every, all, always — are where these items turn. Check them against the stem's exception rates, then look for the option that keeps the claim and fixes the quantifier.

topic: Reporting a unit cost improvement alongside rising total spend
stem: A digital bank's platform team plans to tell the CFO that 'unit cost per thousand tokens fell 31% after the optimisation programme'. Over the same six months, monthly inference spend rose from £84,000 to £119,000, and monthly requests rose from 6.1 million to 12.6 million; average tokens per request were unchanged, so the same 31% improvement holds per request. What should the report say?

options.text: Cost per request fell from £0.0138 to £0.0094 while volume more than doubled, so total monthly spend rose 42% to £119,000.
The 31% unit improvement alone, since total spend is a function of demand and demand is set by product, not by the platform team.
The increase in total spend alone, since that is the figure the CFO's budget carries and unit improvements are an internal engineering matter.
The 31% unit improvement together with the spend the bank would have incurred at the old unit cost, presenting the difference as a saving delivered.

explanation.correct: Both facts are true and each is misleading on its own. Cost per request is the honest unit here because it is denominated in something the CFO recognises, and with tokens per request flat it carries the same 31% improvement while making clear that the total rose because volume grew by more than the efficiency gain absorbed. It is also checkable straight off the ledger: £84,000 over 6.1m requests is £0.0138, £119,000 over 12.6m is £0.0094, a fall of 31%, against spend up 42%. Presenting the pair also frames the right next question — whether request growth is worth what it costs — rather than leaving the CFO to discover the increase from the ledger and distrust the optimisation claim.

distractors.B: Reporting only the improvement while spend rose 42% is the fastest way to lose a CFO's trust, and it will be discovered within one reporting cycle. Disclaiming responsibility for demand also abandons the conversation about whether the growth is worthwhile.
distractors.C: The increase alone implies the optimisation failed, when in fact the bank is now serving more than twice the volume for 42% more money. Suppressing the efficiency gain misrepresents the team's work and removes the basis for funding further optimisation.
distractors.D: A counterfactual avoided cost is a legitimate framing, but leading with it while omitting that actual spend rose is the presentational move most likely to be read as concealment once the budget line is seen. It belongs after the actuals, not instead of them.

explanation.concept: When unit cost falls and total spend rises, report both with a denominator the audience uses. Efficiency and expenditure are separate facts, and presenting either alone invites the audience to conclude the other was hidden.
explanation.tip: Any stem giving you cost, volume and a percentage improvement wants you to compute the per-unit figure and check consistency. Options offering only one side of the picture are wrong regardless of which side.

topic: Cost lines added by a long-horizon retention requirement
stem: A regional health board must retain, for six years, the full prompt, retrieved context and response for every call to its Claude-based referral-letter triage service, to satisfy its clinical records policy. Volume is 30,000 calls a month. Which TWO cost lines does this requirement add that a business case scoped on inference spend would miss? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The per-call token cost of the retrieved context that is sent to the model at request time on every triage call.
The model provider's own logging of these requests, retained on the provider's side under its own policy.
Storage compounding across six years, since retained context dwarfs the responses and the archive never shrinks.
Re-embedding the retained records periodically so the six-year archive stays semantically searchable as the embedding model changes.
Building and operating an access-controlled, tamper-evident path so a specific record can be produced on request.

explanation.correct: A retention requirement is a storage cost and an access cost, and the second is the one business cases forget. Six years of context payloads at 30,000 calls a month accumulate monotonically, and retrieved context dwarfs the responses, so the archive grows on the largest of the three artefacts. Retention is also worthless unless a named record can be produced on request with its integrity demonstrable — which means an access-controlled, tamper-evident retrieval path, built and then operated and periodically tested, for the entire six years.

distractors.A: Context tokens are already inside the inference spend the case was scoped on. The retention requirement does not change what is sent to the model; it changes what happens to a copy afterwards.
distractors.B: Whatever logging the provider performs on its own side is not a cost line the health board carries, and it does not discharge the board's obligation to hold its own records for six years.
distractors.D: Nothing in a records-retention obligation requires semantic search over the archive. Records are produced by identifier or by case reference, so an index keyed on those is sufficient and re-embedding would be spend with no obligation behind it.

explanation.concept: Retention obligations add two recurring lines beyond inference: storage that accumulates for the full period, and a controlled, tamper-evident retrieval capability that must be built, operated and tested. Retained context is usually the largest artefact, so it dominates the volume.
explanation.tip: For retention items, ask what has to happen on the day someone requests a specific record. The production path is a real cost and it is the one that gets left out of the business case.

topic: Vendor challenge answered as a feasibility filter
stem: A Nordic public-sector shared-services organisation runs a Claude-based citizen-correspondence classifier under a published commitment that all processing of citizen data takes place within a named region. A new supplier offers a materially cheaper model, served only from a region outside that commitment. The finance director asks why the team is not switching. What is the strongest response?

options.text: That the cheaper model would classify citizen correspondence less accurately, so the saving would be offset by classification rework.
That the published processing-location commitment is a feasibility filter, not a cost trade-off: a supplier that cannot meet it is not in the comparison set.
That the organisation could route only the correspondence containing no personal data to the cheaper supplier outside the region, capturing part of the saving.
That the payloads could be encrypted before leaving the region, so the published commitment is satisfied while the cheaper supplier is used.

explanation.correct: A published commitment about where processing happens is a constraint on the option set, not a variable to be priced against savings. Framing it that way is what keeps the conversation honest: the finance director is not being told the saving is too small, but that the candidate does not qualify. It also leaves a legitimate path open — the organisation may decide to revisit its published commitment, and that decision has its own consultation, legal review and timeline, which is a separate and much larger conversation than a supplier comparison.

distractors.A: This asserts a quality difference nobody has measured, and it argues on an axis where the supplier can respond with evidence. It also concedes the framing that this is a cost-versus-quality trade-off when the actual blocker is categorical.
distractors.C: Deciding whether an item contains citizen personal data is itself a classification of the content, so the split cannot be made before the content is processed. The proposal is circular and would leak precisely the material the commitment protects.
distractors.D: Residency commitments concern where processing occurs, and the model must receive usable plaintext to classify the correspondence. Encryption in transit and at rest is necessary anyway and does nothing to move the location of processing.

explanation.concept: Distinguish constraints that filter the option set from factors that are traded off within it. A published or regulatory commitment eliminates non-conforming candidates before comparison begins; relaxing it is a separate decision with its own governance, not a line in a cost model.
explanation.tip: When a stem states a published external commitment, expect the answer to be categorical rather than comparative. The distractors will offer clever ways to keep the cheap option inside a constraint that was never negotiable at this level.

topic: Reporting agent quality beyond a final-answer figure
stem: A freight forwarder's Claude-based customs-classification agent completes each case in five tool-using steps: extract the goods description, retrieve tariff candidates, apply exclusion rules, check origin documentation, and issue the classification with justification. Final classifications are correct 88% of the time. The sponsor wants that one figure in a board pack that is asking the board to approve a remediation budget. What should the architect provide?

options.text: The 88% figure alone, since the board is accountable for outcomes rather than for the internals of the agent pipeline.
The product of the five per-step success rates, which gives the true end-to-end accuracy the 88% headline overstates.
The per-step success rates only, since the remediation budget will be spent on individual steps rather than on the pipeline taken as a whole.
The 88% figure with the distribution of failures across the five steps, since two systems at 88% with failures in different steps need different remediation.

explanation.correct: What the board is deciding determines what it needs. Approving remediation spend is a question about where the failures are, and 88% is silent on that. Failures concentrated in tariff retrieval point at the index and the query; failures in origin-document checking point at extraction and evidence handling, and probably carry more compliance exposure. Reporting the outcome figure keeps the board anchored on what the system delivers, and the failure distribution is what makes the budget request evaluable rather than a request to be trusted.

distractors.A: The outcome-only principle holds when the board is judging whether a system is good enough. Here it is being asked to allocate money across remediation options, and a single scalar gives it no basis on which to allocate anything.
distractors.B: Multiplying step success rates assumes independence and no downstream recovery, neither of which holds in an agent that can catch an earlier error at a later step. The measured end-to-end figure is the ground truth, and a lower computed number would simply be wrong.
distractors.C: Per-step figures without the end-to-end result leave the board unable to judge whether the system is acceptable overall or how much the remediation would be expected to move it. Step metrics diagnose; they do not tell you what the system delivers.

explanation.concept: For multi-step agents, report the end-to-end outcome and the failure distribution across steps together. Final-answer accuracy alone cannot direct remediation, and step-level rates cannot be multiplied into an end-to-end figure because steps are neither independent nor free of downstream recovery.
explanation.tip: Let the decision the audience faces set the granularity. An approval of whether to proceed needs the outcome; an allocation of remediation effort needs the outcome plus where the failures sit.
